quiz.why: Without a reaction a hit feels like it skipped off the surface, so at least add FX and SFX (vocal reactions help).

quiz.q: Which is a Rogers QTE best practice?
options: Randomize the prompt's screen position to keep players alert
Always make a failed QTE an instant death
Use QTEs for every attack to look cool
Keep the button prompt in the same screen location
quiz.why: A consistent prompt position avoids confusion. Rogers prefers heavy damage over instant death and says to reserve QTEs for big moments.

quiz.q: A player fails a QTE they reached after three attack patterns. What should happen?
options: Repeat one pattern, then retry the QTE
Skip the QTE and award the kill
quiz.why: Get them back to the QTE quickly: repeat one set, not all three. Auto-awarding removes the challenge entirely.

quiz.q: What happened with shields across Maximo 1 and Maximo 2?
options: The unbreakable shield in the sequel made players block far more
The breakable shield in the original was used constantly
Players asked for the shield to be removed
The sequel made the shield a consumable
quiz.why: Players hoarded the breakable shield in Maximo 1 and dodged instead. Making it unbreakable in Maximo 2 encouraged blocking.

quiz.q: Your F2P players stockpile premium boosters and almost never use them. Which book lesson fits best?
options: Maximo's breakable shield: limited resources get hoarded
quiz.why: Scarcity makes players save items 'for later'. Make them more plentiful or regenerating so players use them and feel their value.

quiz.q: Why must stealth kills only work under specific conditions?
options: Otherwise players spam them over regular attacks as an exploit
Rating boards forbid frequent stealth kills
quiz.why: Without conditions (position, cover, shadow) the cool move becomes an exploit and goes stale.

quiz.q: Which lock-on marker is NOT one of the four the book shows?
quiz.why: The book shows floor marker, pointer arrow, glowing aura and a health bar over the target. A minimap ping isn't one of them.

quiz.q: A dodge in your action game sometimes leaves players inside explosion radiuses. Which rule is broken?
options: The camera must pass through hazards
Dodge metrics must fully clear wide, long and radius attacks
quiz.why: Mind your metrics: dodges must completely clear wide attacks, long weapons and radius effects, or players do the 'graveyard hustle'.

quiz.q: The Three As of projectile combat are:
quiz.why: Action (load, fire, unload), Aiming (sighting the target), Ammo (what's fired).

quiz.q: In the book's weapon matrix, which weapon is 'very strong' at long range?
quiz.why: The sniper rifle owns long range. The assault rifle owns medium and the shotgun owns short, so overlap is minimal.

quiz.q: What's Hardy LeBel's advice on ranged weapon power?
options: Make ranged weapons weak so the player isn't overpowered
Be generous: players expect ranged combat to feel powerful
quiz.why: LeBel warns that weakening ranged weapons to offset perceived power is a common mistake. Be generous.

quiz.q: Lots of cover, frequent line-of-sight breaks and regenerating health produce what rhythm?
options: Swirling dogfights of engage and disengage
quiz.why: That's LeBel's dogfight recipe. Long corridors plus high lethality produce cautious play instead.

quiz.q: A shooter player runs out of ammo. What does Rogers say they should always have?
quiz.why: Being unable to fight back feels powerless, so give a knife, fists, pistol-whip or rifle butt (Gears even has a chainsaw).

quiz.q: Which is a correct smart bomb guideline?
options: Let it charge as fast as possible
Hide its controls to keep it a surprise
It should damage the player too
It destroys everything on screen except the player, and players should see what they're charging toward
quiz.why: Smart bombs clear the screen (destructibles included) but must be rationed and clearly signposted, or encounters get wiped out.

quiz.q: What's Rogers' guidance on poison and antidotes?
options: Make the antidote more common than the poison
Make antidotes rarer than poison for tension
Poison should have no visual so it surprises players
quiz.why: Poison should be readable and survivable. Never make death feel inevitable; always give a fighting chance.

quiz.q: The player should survive 20 hits and the average enemy hit deals 10. Starting health?
quiz.why: Rogers' formula: hits x damage per hit = 20 x 10 = 200.

quiz.q: Where did lives and game-over screens come from, per Rogers?
quiz.why: Arcades wanted quarters fast; extra lives kept players paying. On paid home games that logic no longer applies.

quiz.q: The player dies during a long boss fight. Rogers' recommendation?
options: Remove the boss after three deaths
Let the fight continue, or restore just a little boss health
Double the boss's health as a penalty
quiz.why: Don't make them replay everything. Continue as if nothing happened, or at most regain a bit of boss health.

quiz.q: Your F2P game's D1 retention is fine, but players quit at level 12 after repeated failures, a long fail animation and an expensive continue. Which principle is most violated?
options: Give your character a signature weapon
Keep the player playing: fast restarts, no reason to stop
quiz.why: Rogers: never give players a good reason to stop. Kill quickly, restart fast, don't punish. Level 12 has become a churn cliff.

quiz.q: In a gacha PvP mode, one team can chain-stun the other until death. Which Rogers truth addresses this?
options: Always strive to enable the player, even when disabling them
quiz.why: Disables should leave a way out. CC immunity windows or diminishing returns apply this rule to PvP.

quiz.q: Auto-battle in mobile RPGs most directly extends which Rogers idea?
options: Batman never misses, so the player shouldn't either: make players look cool
quiz.why: Like Arkham's choreographed combat, auto-battle guarantees flawless execution, and skill moves to team-building and decisions.

sideQuests.title: Matrix Me
sideQuests.task: Pick a Brawl Stars brawler or a Clash Royale card you know. Fill Rogers' 7 attack-matrix columns for its attacks, then add 3 F2P columns: cost/cooldown, counters, rarity.

sideQuests.title: Spatula of Destiny
sideQuests.task: Pick an absurd weapon (garden hose, umbrella, rubber chicken). Brainstorm 10 combat and non-combat uses covering at least 3 ranges and 2 elevations.

sideQuests.title: Juice Audit
sideQuests.task: Play 3 minutes of a mobile combat game with sound on, then 3 minutes muted. List every feedback element (hit-stop, numbers, haptics, flashes, sounds). What breaks when muted?

sideQuests.title: Weapon Venn
sideQuests.task: Design 4 weapons for a hypothetical mobile shooter. Fill a short/medium/long matrix so each range has exactly one 'very strong' weapon and every overlap pays a cost.

sideQuests.title: Rewrite the Fail Screen
sideQuests.task: Screenshot a mobile game's fail or continue screen. Mark what's ethical and what's pressure, then sketch a fairer version using Rogers' 'keep going' screen and death rules.

sideQuests.title: CC Fairness Check
sideQuests.task: List every disable effect in a game you play (stun, knockback, freeze...). For each, write how the player escapes or counters it. Flag any with no counter.

sideQuests.title: Health Math
sideQuests.task: Use Rogers' formula to set a level-1 hero's HP. Then predict what happens over 10 levels if enemy damage grows 15% per level while hero HP grows 10%.

mainQuests.title: The Combat One-Pager for a Mobile Game
mainQuests.task: Design the combat for an original F2P mobile game (survivor-like, hero brawler or auto-battler). Cover: personality to signature weapon; an attack matrix with 5+ moves (Rogers' 7 columns plus cost/cooldown and counter); ranges and elevations with a range-diagram sketch; a feel plan (chain timing, one heavy wind-up attack, 5 mobile juice elements); one enemy disable and how the player escapes it; your health formula; and your fail-state and revive policy with an ethics statement.
mainQuests.deliverable: A one-page combat design doc with an attack matrix table and a range sketch.
mainQuests.doneWhen: Every matrix row is distinct, every disable has a counter, the fail flow returns to gameplay in 2 taps or fewer, each choice cites a Rogers principle, and it's posted publicly for feedback.

mainQuests.title: Revive Offer Teardown
mainQuests.task: Compare the fail/continue flows of 3 F2P games (e.g. a match-3, a runner, a roguelite or survivor-like). For each, record time from death to retry, offer price and currency, ad option, cap per run, what you lose by declining, and a 1-5 fairness score based on Rogers' death rules.
mainQuests.deliverable: A comparison table with screenshots, one 'steal this' and one 'never do this' per game, plus a 3-sentence conclusion.
mainQuests.doneWhen: All 3 games are scored with evidence, and the conclusion states what makes a revive feel fair.

playLabs.question: Which of Hardy LeBel's rhythm factors does Brawl Stars lean on most, and how does the map change fights?

playLabs.lookFor: Which attack shapes (straight, diagonal, radial, area) your skills cover, how the game creates close-battle tension despite hordes, and what the death or revive screen offers.
playLabs.question: When did you feel most in danger, and was the revive offer fair by Rogers' death rules?

playLabs.game: Honkai: Star Rail or AFK Journey
playLabs.lookFor: One fight played manually and one on auto: where the decisions live (team, weakness/element, ultimate timing) and whether cinematics can be skipped.
playLabs.question: What does the game still ask YOU to decide on auto, and how does it show why you won or lost?

playLabs.game: Candy Crush Saga or Royal Match
playLabs.lookFor: The continue offer when you run out of moves: price, the size of the 'no thanks' option, lives, and how fast you can retry.
playLabs.question: Which of Rogers' death rules does it follow, and which does it bend for monetization?

retrieval.q: What are Liddell Hart's three elements of combat?
Give Rogers' two reasons violent games get so much attention, and the loop behind the second.
retrieval.a: Violence is graphic, dramatic and visceral, so it gives the quickest positive feedback loop: action, immediate result, reward (Freud's pleasure principle).

retrieval.q: List the questions for judging how violent your game feels.
retrieval.a: Does the player do it, with realistic weapons? How often? Is it rewarded or shown as inappropriate? How graphic (dismemberment, lingering)? Any residue (blood, gibs)? Is it against bad guys, and do enemies suffer?

retrieval.q: Name the four ranges and four elevations of combat.
retrieval.a: Ranges: close, medium, long, area effect. Elevations: standing, low, high, aerial.

retrieval.q: What columns belong in an attack matrix?
retrieval.a: Name, control scheme, range, speed, direction, damage (label plus number or %), special, plus extra columns as needed.

retrieval.q: How does a combat chain work, and why must the hero translate forward?
retrieval.a: Three or more moves; pressing within about a second continues to stronger hits. Forward movement keeps knocked-back enemies in reach.
On heavy or oversized weapons: risk the wait for a devastating payoff (risk vs reward).
Reserve them for bombastic attacks (single-button finishers are fine); same prompt location; a beat to react; quick return after failure; heavy damage rather than instant death.

retrieval.q: What did Maximo teach about shields?
retrieval.a: A breakable shield got hoarded and avoided; an unbreakable one made players block happily.

retrieval.q: What are the Three As, with one question each?
retrieval.a: Action (manual or auto reload?), Aiming (auto-aim or free aim, scope obstruction?), Ammo (carry limits, special rounds, what misses do?).

retrieval.q: What does the book's weapon matrix teach?
retrieval.a: Each range has one 'very strong' weapon (shotgun short, assault rifle medium, sniper long); minimal overlap, and overlap carries a cost.

retrieval.q: Name the seven control-loss states and one caution.
retrieval.a: Stun, knockback, knockdown, latching, transformation, loss of balance, sliding. Use them judiciously, avoid double bolting, end transformations quickly, always leave an escape.
Hits the player can take before losing a life without healing, times average enemy damage: 20 x 10 = 200.

retrieval.q: List Rogers' rules for killing the player.
retrieval.a: Tell them about lives; show lives clearly; offer ways to regain lives; kill quickly; short game over and fast restart; death as violent as the rating allows; no double punishment; boss fights continue; use the threat wisely; make partner-death rules clear.

retrieval.q: What is the 'keep going' screen, and how does F2P use it?
retrieval.a: It replaces game over with a preview of what's next. F2P fail screens show progress and next rewards; honest when transparent, predatory with rigged near-misses or pressure timers.
